title: podlake load: high memory + slow on large loads (wide MARC schema)
description:
Observed while testing: `podlake load` of ~2M Brown records used ~8 GB RAM (~20% on the test box) and took a good chunk of time. Not even a large set.

## Likely root cause
The marctable schema is extremely wide — hundreds/~1000 all-VARCHAR columns (a column per MARC field tag and every field+subfield combo), mostly null. 2M rows x ~1000 columns ~= ~2B cells, which DuckDB buffers into row groups and rewrites as partitioned, snappy-compressed DuckLake Parquet during INSERT ... FROM read_parquet(). DuckDB's default memory_limit is ~80% of system RAM, so it uses a lot when available (8 GB was well under that cap, so it's not even memory-bound). Largely expected given the schema, but worth reducing.

## Investigate / options
- Set PRAGMA memory_limit and/or threads in lake.connect() to cap RAM.
- Batched inserts (chunk the read_parquet -> insert) instead of one large INSERT.
- Revisit the schema: drop all-null columns, or use a narrower/typed schema instead of ~1000 sparse VARCHAR columns.
- Note: the same wide-schema cost also drives the convert --batch-size memory (already exposed as a flag).
- Applies regardless of OAI vs ResourceSync ingestion.

## Files
- src/podlake/lake.py (load_parquet, _insert_parquet, connect)
- src/podlake/convert.py (_make_columns)

comments.author: edsu
comments.text:
Benchmarked the cause (synthetic 400-col x 1M-row sparse VARCHAR parquet, 315 MB), peak RSS via /usr/bin/time -l:

- non-partitioned INSERT: ~14.0 GB peak RSS
- PARTITIONED BY (org): ~21.5 GB peak RSS  (+~50%)
- non-partitioned + preserve_insertion_order=false: ~13.7 GB (no real help)
- partitioned + memory_limit=4GB: ~5.7 GB RSS but ~8.7 GB spilled to temp

So peak RAM is cappable with memory_limit, but that just shifts the cost to disk spill + time. At real scale (~2M rows x ~1000 cols ~= 5x this test) that scales to the observed ~90 GB spill / ~2 hours. A 315 MB parquet expanding to a ~14 GB working set is a ~44x blowup — the root cause is the ~1000-column sparse all-VARCHAR schema, not a tuning bug.

Levers (marginal): drop PARTITIONED BY (org) (saves ~50%; single-org files still prune via file min/max stats); set a memory_limit to avoid OOM (trades RAM for spill/time).

Durable fix (bigger change): narrow the schema — e.g. store MARC as one serialized column (marcxml/json) plus a few extracted columns, or only emit populated columns instead of ~1000 mostly-null ones.

IMPORTANT: this affects the ResourceSync sync path too (PR #6) — a first-time `sync` of a large org's full dump runs the same wide INSERT.

comments.author: edsu
comments.text: Addressed by the long/EAV redesign (branch narrow-schema): records is now a tall one-row-per-subfield table + a small record_meta table, dropping the wide ~2366-column schema (and the marctable dependency). Benchmark on the same Brown data: load dropped from ~2 h / ~90 GB spill to ~2 s / <1 GB. Verified end-to-end on real POD data (EAV queries + lossless reconstruction incl. the leader). Close when the PR merges.

title: Evaluate converting MARCXML parsing to mrrc (Rust)
description:
Now that the EAV redesign made the DuckLake load cheap (podlake-h9w), MARC **parsing** is the dominant cost of convert/sync/fetch. Evaluated mrrc (dchud/mrrc, a Rust MARC library with pip-installable Python bindings, ~pymarc-compatible) as a faster parser behind podlake's parse seam (convert._iter_marcxml_records). Outcome: **deferred** — a modest win with non-trivial friction. Details below so we can pick it up later.

## Findings (mrrc 0.9.1; `pip install mrrc`)

**Gate 1 — parses POD MARCXML correctly: PASS.** `mrrc.xml_to_records(xml_str)` returned correct leader, control fields, 245 subfields, and indicators; `is_control_field()` exists.

**Gate 2 — goldrush(mrrc_record): FAILS out of the box.** `TypeError: 'method' object is not iterable`. Root cause: mrrc exposes `record.fields()` and `field.subfields()` as **methods**, whereas pymarc (and goldrush, and podlake's convert.record_to_rows) treat `record.fields` / `field.subfields` as **attributes**. Fixable — goldrush is ours (edsu) — but the same mismatch means record_to_rows must also be adapted to mrrc's method API. So it is NOT a pure parser swap.

**Throughput benchmark (MARCXML):** ~150k real Brown records (replicated), single-threaded:
- current lxml.iterparse + pymarc: ~4,000 rec/s
- mrrc.xml_to_records:            ~9,400 rec/s  (**~2.3x**)
Note this is far from the ~8x mrrc advertises — that figure is for *binary* MARC per-record reads, not MARCXML.

**Memory caveat (important):** `xml_to_records` takes the *entire* XML as one string and returns the *entire* `list[Record]` — no streaming. For a full dump (~5 GB decompressed for Brown) that holds the whole string + all Record objects in memory, versus our constant-memory `lxml.iterparse`. mrrc's streaming/parallel APIs (MARCReader, parse_batch_parallel) are for *binary* MARC, not XML. Solvable by having podlake split the gz stream into record batches and call `xml_to_records` per batch — but that's extra integration.

**Only part of convert:** swapping the parser does not touch goldrush (per-record match-key CPU), EAV row-building, or the Parquet write. So a 2.3x on parsing yields a smaller end-to-end convert win — estimated ~1.3-1.7x. **Decisive next measurement before adopting: profile a real convert to see parse's actual share** (if ~30%, mrrc caps around ~1.2x overall and is not worth it).

## Why deferred
Parsing is not a blocker (unlike the load, which EAV fixed). The overall win is modest and the costs are real: an experimental dependency, a batching layer to preserve bounded memory, method-API adaptation in record_to_rows, and a goldrush change.

## Revisit triggers
- Initial-load parse time becomes a practical pain, OR
- mrrc gains a streaming MARCXML reader (constant memory + Rust speed).

## Integration path if adopted
- Keep the parse seam (convert._iter_marcxml_records); feed mrrc batched `xml_to_records` to bound memory.
- Adapt convert.record_to_rows to mrrc's method API (fields(), subfields(), field.data / control_fields()).
- Update goldrush to accept records whose fields/subfields are methods (or add an adapter).
- Add mrrc as a dependency (currently experimental). Local checkout: /Users/edsu/Projects/mrrc.
